title: The Algorithm Knows Me Better Than I'd Like
script: Narrator: [wry] I used to boast that I only opened my social feed for five minutes at a time, which, in hindsight, was a fairly generous estimate of my own self-control.
Narrator: [reflective] What I hadn't accounted for was that the feed wasn't neutral; it had been quietly studying me for years, learning exactly which images made my thumb pause mid-scroll.
Narrator: [candid] Outrage, it turns out, is remarkably efficient. A clip of a stranger behaving badly could hold my attention far longer than anything genuinely useful ever managed to.
Narrator: [unsettled] Had someone told me a decade ago that I'd spend an evening furious at a person I'd never met, over a controversy that would be forgotten by morning, I'd have laughed them off.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Yet there I was, night after night, feeling as though I were staying informed, when in reality I was simply being fed whatever kept me twitching my thumb.
Narrator: [honest] The turning point came when I noticed I could recall dozens of arguments I'd witnessed online, yet almost nothing I'd read in the book gathering dust on my nightstand.

Narrator: [determined] So I did something deliberately inconvenient: I deleted the app and left only the browser version, which loads slowly enough that my irritation usually wins before the outrage does.
Narrator: [wry] The first week felt like withdrawal, which sounds dramatic until you consider how deliberately these feeds are engineered to make withdrawal feel exactly like that.
Narrator: [reflective] Gradually, though, I noticed my thoughts slowing down, becoming less reactive, less inclined to assume the worst about strangers based on fifteen seconds of context.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I've since realized that being informed and being provoked are two entirely different sensations that the algorithm is happy to let me confuse indefinitely.
Narrator: [warm] Nowadays, if something online makes my pulse spike within seconds, I treat that reaction as a warning label rather than a reason to keep scrolling.
Narrator: [candid] I'm under no illusion that I've escaped it entirely; the pull is still there, quieter now, waiting patiently for the moment my guard slips.
Narrator: [with a small smile] But at least these days, when my attention gets hijacked, I notice it happening, which apparently counts as progress in this particular battle.

quiz.question: What does the narrator realize the feed had been doing for years?
options: Recommending books to her
Quietly studying her to learn what made her pause while scrolling
Sending her advertisements only
Blocking content she disliked
quiz.explanation: She realizes the feed had been quietly studying her to learn exactly which images made her thumb pause mid-scroll.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say is remarkably efficient at holding attention?
options: Educational videos
Outrage, such as a clip of a stranger behaving badly
Music playlists
Weather updates
quiz.explanation: She says outrage is remarkably efficient, giving the example of a clip of a stranger behaving badly.

quiz.question: What was the turning point that made her reconsider her habits?
options: She lost her phone
She noticed she recalled online arguments but almost nothing from the book by her bed
A friend confronted her
She ran out of storage space
quiz.explanation: She noticed she could recall dozens of online arguments but almost nothing from the book gathering dust on her nightstand.

quiz.question: What deliberately inconvenient step did she take?
options: She bought a new phone
She deleted the app and kept only the slower-loading browser version
She gave her phone to a friend
She stopped using the internet entirely
quiz.explanation: She deleted the app and left only the browser version, which loads slowly enough that irritation often wins before outrage does.

quiz.question: How does she now treat a sudden spike in her pulse while scrolling?
options: As a sign to keep scrolling faster
As a warning label rather than a reason to keep scrolling
As proof the content is trustworthy
She ignores the feeling completely
quiz.explanation: She now treats a fast pulse as a warning label rather than a reason to keep scrolling.
